alignment.note: Greek uses an aorist participle προελθών ('having gone forward'); the Vulgate renders this with a temporal clause cum processisset, while the Peshitta employs a finite verb ܘܩܪܒ ('and he drew near') from the root q-r-b, coordinated rather than subordinated. The Peshitta verb also shifts sense slightly from 'going forward' to 'drawing near'.

Greek ἔπιπτεν is imperfect ('he was falling'), suggesting durative or repeated action; the Peshitta ܘܢܦܠ (root n-p-l) and Vulgate procidit render it as a simple finite past, losing the iterative aspectual nuance of the Greek imperfect.

Greek προσηύχετο is a single imperfect middle verb; the Peshitta renders the durative force periphrastically with the participle ܡܨܠܐ plus the auxiliary ܗܘܐ ('was praying'), a characteristic Syriac construction for the imperfect/continuous aspect.

The Greek conditional particle εἰ and the conjunction ἵνα are both present; the Peshitta fuses the purpose and condition into the single proclitic ܕܐܢ ('that if'), economising on the two separate Greek particles.

Greek δυνατόν ἐστιν ('it is possible') and Vulgate fieri posset ('it could be done') express the possibility impersonally; the Peshitta uses the single participle ܡܫܟܚܐ (root sh-k-kh, lit. 'is able/found possible'), a typical Syriac idiom for impersonal possibility.

Greek ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ ('from him') is rendered analytically; the Peshitta contracts the preposition and pronoun into the single suffixed form ܡܢܗ ('from him'), reflecting the agglutinative morphology of Syriac. The Greek article ἡ before ὥρα has no equivalent in Syriac or Latin, both lacking the definite article here.
